sources.note: Overview of WCAG, ATAG, UAAG and ARIA.

question: An auditor must assess a 20,000-page website for WCAG conformance and cannot check every page. According to WCAG-EM, what should they do?
options: Test only the home page, since it represents the whole site
Rely on an automated scan, since it covers every criterion
Test only the pages that get the most traffic
Explore the site, then test a structured and random sample
rationale: WCAG-EM, the W3C's WCAG Evaluation Methodology, has five steps: define the scope, explore the product, select a representative sample, evaluate the sample, and report the findings. When checking everything isn't practical, the sample should include key pages, common functions, different types of content and templates, plus some randomly chosen pages to check the result. This gives a defensible basis for a conformance claim about a whole site.

distractors.0: One page can't represent the templates, functions and content types across a large site.
distractors.1: Automated tools check only part of WCAG; many criteria need human judgment. WCAG-EM is a manual method, which tools can support.
distractors.2: Traffic alone misses important but less visited pages, such as forms or account pages. WCAG-EM combines structured and random selection.

sources.title: W3C WAI: WCAG-EM Overview
sources.note: The five steps of the evaluation methodology and the WCAG-EM Report Tool.

question: In the W3C Accessibility Maturity Model, an organization has a roadmap and a defined, organized approach to accessibility, but it is not yet embedded and continuously evaluated across the whole organization. Which maturity level is this?
options: Inactive
Launch
Integrate
Optimize
rationale: The W3C Accessibility Maturity Model describes four cumulative levels. Inactive means little or no awareness. Launch means the need is recognized and planning has begun, but activities are not well organized. Integrate means there is a roadmap and the overall approach is defined and organized. Optimize means accessibility runs through the whole organization and is regularly evaluated and improved. The model assesses seven dimensions: communications, oversight and culture, the ICT development life cycle, knowledge and skills, personnel, procurement, and support.

distractors.0: Inactive describes an organization with little awareness of accessibility. This organization already has a roadmap.
distractors.1: Launch is the stage where planning has started but work is not yet well organized. A defined, organized approach is a step beyond it.
distractors.3: Optimize is the highest level, where accessibility is embedded everywhere and assessed consistently. The scenario says that is not yet true.

tip: Inactive → Launch → Integrate → Optimize. Maturity is measured per dimension, so an organization can be at different levels in different areas.

sources.title: W3C: Accessibility Maturity Model
sources.note: Group Note describing the seven dimensions and four maturity levels.

question: According to W3C guidance, who is the main audience for an organization's accessibility statement, and what must it include?
options: Users; it needs a commitment, the standard and a contact
Lawyers; it needs a full legal defense against complaints
Developers; it needs code samples for each known fix
Investors; it needs the cost of all accessibility work
rationale: An accessibility statement is written mainly for users, who often read it when they hit a problem. W3C recommends at minimum a commitment to accessibility, the standard applied (such as WCAG 2.2 AA), and contact details for feedback. Known limitations and alternatives are also recommended so users aren't surprised. Plain language works better than technical or legal wording: 'some videos have no captions' helps a user more than a criterion number.

distractors.1: A statement is a communication to users, not a legal brief. Legal jargon makes it less useful.
distractors.2: Technical detail belongs in internal documentation. The statement explains accessibility to the people using the content.
distractors.3: Costs are an internal planning concern, not part of a public accessibility statement.

sources.title: W3C WAI: Developing an Accessibility Statement
sources.note: Required and recommended contents, plus a statement generator.

question: A product team plans to have one blind employee review their app just before launch and treat that as their accessibility testing. What is the main weakness of this plan?
options: Blind users can't evaluate mobile apps in a useful way
Involving users is only worthwhile after a product launches
One person can't represent everyone, and launch is too late
User feedback isn't accepted as evidence under WCAG
rationale: W3C recommends involving users with a range of disabilities early and throughout a project: in planning, personas and walkthroughs, prototype reviews, and evaluation. One person can't speak for how others with the same disability use technology, let alone other disabilities. Leaving it to the end means problems are found when they are most expensive to fix. User involvement works best alongside standards like WCAG and a conformance evaluation, not as a replacement for them.

distractors.0: Blind people use mobile apps every day with built-in screen readers, and their feedback is valuable.
distractors.1: W3C says the opposite: involve users from the start, when findings are cheapest to act on.
distractors.3: WCAG conformance is judged against its success criteria, but user feedback is a recommended part of good practice. That is not the main weakness of this plan.

sources.title: W3C WAI: Involving Users in Web Projects for Better, Easier Accessibility
sources.note: Why and when to involve users with disabilities, and the limits of relying on one person.

question: An organization is writing a web accessibility policy. Which set of elements does W3C guidance recommend it include?
options: A list of the organization's employees with disabilities
The standard and level, the scope, and a timeline
A promise to be fully accessible to everyone immediately
Only a reference to the national law, with no other detail
rationale: W3C suggests that a policy name the standard (for example WCAG) and the conformance level (AA is the most widely adopted), define its scope (public sites, intranets, mobile apps, third-party content, authoring tools), and set a realistic timeline with measurable milestones. Fuller policies also assign responsibilities to specific departments and include a way to review progress and respond to user feedback. A clear policy turns a general commitment into something teams can plan and be held to.

distractors.0: Employee disability information is private and has nothing to do with a content accessibility policy.
distractors.2: W3C advises setting realistic, measurable targets. An unrealistic promise undermines credibility and gives teams no plan.
distractors.3: Laws often lack the detail teams need, and some content may fall outside legal scope. A useful policy states its own standard, scope and timeline.

sources.title: W3C WAI: Developing Organizational Policies on Web Accessibility
sources.note: Policy elements: standards, conformance level, scope, timeline and responsibilities.

question: W3C's "Planning and Managing Web Accessibility" groups activities into four phases. In which phase does an organization develop a business case, raise awareness and gather support?
options: Implement
Sustain
Plan
Initiate
rationale: The four phases are Initiate, Plan, Implement and Sustain. Initiate is about building understanding and enthusiasm: learning the basics, exploring the current situation, setting objectives, developing a business case, raising awareness and gathering support. Plan then creates the policy, assigns responsibilities and sets budget and monitoring. Implement builds skills, integrates accessibility into processes and evaluates early. Sustain keeps monitoring, tracks changes in standards and law, and acts on user feedback.

distractors.0: Implement is when staff are trained, tools are in place and accessibility is built into work. It comes after support has been secured.
distractors.1: Sustain is about ongoing monitoring and improvement once accessibility is in place.
distractors.2: Plan is where the policy, responsibilities, budget and monitoring framework are set. It follows Initiate.

sources.title: W3C WAI: Planning and Managing Web Accessibility
sources.note: The Initiate, Plan, Implement and Sustain phases and their activities.

question: A team uses W3C's Accessibility Roles and Responsibilities Mapping (ARRM) to decide who owns writing text alternatives for images. What does it mean to give the content author the "primary" role for that task?
options: The author should be consulted, but someone else decides
The author helps complete the task but is not accountable
The author must approve the task before launch, but not do it
The author is ultimately accountable for the task being done
rationale: ARRM helps teams map each WCAG-related task to the project roles that own it, such as content authors, UX designers, visual designers and front-end developers. Each task has a primary owner, who is ultimately accountable; secondary owners, who share responsibility and help complete it; and contributors, whose input should be sought. Clear ownership stops accessibility work from falling between roles, a common reason it gets missed.

distractors.0: Being consulted describes the contributor role.
distractors.1: Helping without being accountable describes the secondary role.
distractors.2: ARRM has no approver role. Its levels are primary, secondary and contributor.

sources.title: W3C WAI: Accessibility Roles and Responsibilities Mapping (ARRM)
sources.note: How ARRM assigns primary, secondary and contributor ownership of accessibility tasks.

question: A web page has a purely decorative swirl image between sections. How should it be handled to meet WCAG 1.1.1 Non-text Content?
options: Give it alt text that describes the swirl's shape and colors
Hide it from assistive technology, for example with an empty alt attribute
Add a visible caption below the image explaining what it is
Give it a short alt text that just says "image"
rationale: Success criterion 1.1.1 (Level A) requires text alternatives for meaningful non-text content, but decorative images are handled differently: they must be implemented so assistive technology can ignore them. In HTML that usually means alt="" (null alt), or placing the image in CSS. Describing decoration wastes screen reader users' time and adds noise. The skill being tested is judging purpose: the same picture can need a description in one context and none in another.

distractors.0: Describing decoration makes screen reader users listen to content that carries no information, which is exactly what the criterion tries to avoid.
distractors.2: A visible caption adds clutter for everyone and still exposes the decoration to assistive technology.
distractors.3: Placeholder alt text like "image" is a known WCAG failure. It tells the user nothing and stops the image being ignored.

tip: Ask what the image is for. Informative: describe the information. Functional (a link or button): describe the action. Decorative: hide it.

sources.title: Understanding SC 1.1.1 Non-text Content
sources.note: Intent, decorative images, and related techniques and failures.

question: A designer makes section titles look like headings by using large bold text, but marks them up as ordinary paragraphs. Which WCAG success criterion does this fail?
options: 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)
2.4.7 Focus Visible
1.3.1 Info and Relationships
3.1.1 Language of Page
rationale: Success criterion 1.3.1 (Level A) requires that structure and relationships shown visually, such as headings, lists, table headers and form labels, are also available in code. Large bold text looks like a heading to sighted users, but a screen reader announces it as plain text, and users can't jump between headings. Using real heading elements makes the same structure available to everyone. W3C lists using presentation alone to convey structure as a failure of this criterion.

distractors.0: Contrast is about the lightness difference between text and background. The problem here is missing structure, not readability.
distractors.1: Focus Visible is about seeing which element has keyboard focus. Headings are not focusable controls.
distractors.3: Language of Page is about declaring the page's human language so screen readers pronounce it correctly.

tip: If sighted users get meaning from layout or styling, ask whether that meaning is in the code too. If not, think 1.3.1.

sources.title: Understanding SC 1.3.1 Info and Relationships
sources.note: Intent, examples with headings, labels and tables, and related failures.

question: A form marks required fields only by turning their labels red. Which change would satisfy WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color?
options: Switch to a brighter, more saturated red
Make the required labels green instead of red
Add a tooltip saying "required" that appears on mouse hover
Add a visible asterisk, explained in the form instructions
rationale: Success criterion 1.4.1 (Level A) says color must not be the only visual means of conveying information. People with color vision deficiencies, people with low vision and anyone using a monochrome display may not see the red. Adding a visible marker, such as an asterisk or the word "required", gives a second cue that doesn't depend on color. Color can still be used, as long as it isn't the only cue.

distractors.0: A brighter red still relies on color alone. Contrast doesn't help someone who can't tell red from other colors.
distractors.1: Changing the color keeps the same problem. Red-green color blindness is the most common type, so green may be even worse.
distractors.2: A hover tooltip isn't available to keyboard or touch users and isn't visible until the user acts. The cue needs to be visible.

sources.title: Understanding SC 1.4.1 Use of Color
sources.note: Intent and examples, including required form fields and links.

question: Under WCAG 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), what contrast ratio does normal-size body text need against its background?
options: At least 4.5:1
At least 3:1
At least 7:1
At least 2:1
rationale: Success criterion 1.4.3 (Level AA) requires at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text, meaning at least 18 point, or 14 point bold. Logos and incidental text, such as text in inactive controls or pure decoration, are exempt. Enough contrast helps people with low vision or reduced contrast sensitivity, which becomes common with age. It also helps anyone reading a screen in bright light.

distractors.1: 3:1 is the minimum for large text under 1.4.3, not for normal body text.
distractors.2: 7:1 is the enhanced requirement for normal text under 1.4.6, which is Level AAA.
distractors.3: 2:1 is below every WCAG text contrast requirement.

tip: Memorize 4.5 / 3 / 7: AA normal text, AA large text, AAA normal text.

sources.title: Understanding SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)
sources.note: Ratios, the definition of large text, and exceptions.

question: WCAG 1.4.4 Resize Text requires that text can be enlarged to what level without assistive technology and without loss of content or functionality?
rationale: Success criterion 1.4.4 (Level AA) requires that text can be resized up to 200% using the browser's or platform's built-in features, such as zoom or text-size settings, without content being cut off or controls breaking. Captions and images of text are excluded. It supports people with low vision who need larger text but don't use a screen magnifier.

distractors.0: 150% is less than WCAG requires.
distractors.2: 400% is the zoom level tied to 1.4.10 Reflow, where content must work at a width of 320 CSS pixels. It is a different criterion.
distractors.3: No WCAG criterion sets 800%.

tip: 200% for Resize Text, 400% for Reflow.

sources.title: Understanding SC 1.4.4 Resize Text
sources.note: Intent and the 200% requirement.

question: A user with low vision zooms a desktop page to 400% and has to scroll left and right to read every line. Which WCAG success criterion addresses this?
options: 1.4.4 Resize Text
2.4.1 Bypass Blocks
1.4.10 Reflow
1.3.4 Orientation
rationale: Success criterion 1.4.10 (Level AA) requires content to be usable at a width of 320 CSS pixels, which matches a 1280-pixel-wide window zoomed to 400%, without scrolling in two directions. Scrolling both ways on every line is slow and makes it easy to lose your place. Content that needs a two-dimensional layout, such as maps, data tables or video, is excepted. Responsive layouts that collapse into a single column usually meet it, and they help phone users too.

distractors.0: Resize Text is about enlarging text to 200%. Reflow is the criterion about horizontal scrolling at high zoom.
distractors.1: Bypass Blocks is about skipping repeated content such as navigation menus.
distractors.3: Orientation is about not locking content to portrait or landscape. It doesn't cover zoom.

sources.title: Understanding SC 1.4.10 Reflow
sources.note: The 320 CSS pixel requirement, exceptions and who benefits.

question: A training video shows on-screen steps that the narrator never says aloud. Which WCAG requirement ensures blind viewers get that information?
options: Audio description (1.2.5)
Captions (1.2.2)
Sign language interpretation (1.2.6)
Pause, Stop, Hide (2.2.2)
rationale: Success criterion 1.2.5 Audio Description (Prerecorded), Level AA, requires narration of important visual information that the soundtrack doesn't already convey, such as actions, scene changes and on-screen text. The narration is added during natural pauses in the dialogue. It benefits people who are blind or have low vision, and some people with cognitive disabilities who find it hard to interpret visual events. If the main narration already describes everything important, no extra description is needed.

distractors.1: Captions turn audio into text for Deaf and hard of hearing viewers. They don't describe visual content.
distractors.2: Sign language interpretation (Level AAA) serves Deaf viewers who use sign language. It is visual, so it doesn't help blind viewers.
distractors.3: Pause, Stop, Hide gives users control over moving or auto-updating content. It doesn't make visual information available as audio.

tip: Captions make sound visible; audio description makes visuals audible.

sources.title: Understanding SC 1.2.5 Audio Description (Prerecorded)
sources.note: Intent and who benefits.

question: An online form logs users out after 5 minutes. Which approach satisfies WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable?
options: Show a countdown timer so users know how long they have left
Raise the timeout to 10 minutes for every user of the form
Let users ask for more time by phoning or emailing support
Warn users before time runs out and let them extend it simply
rationale: Success criterion 2.2.1 (Level A) requires that for each time limit, users can turn it off, adjust it to at least ten times the default, or be warned before it expires and given at least 20 seconds to extend it with a simple action, at least ten times. Exceptions cover real-time events like auctions, limits that are essential to the activity, and limits over 20 hours. Time limits are a major barrier for people who read slowly, use assistive technology, or have motor or cognitive disabilities.

distractors.0: A countdown informs users but doesn't give them any way to get more time.
distractors.1: A fixed longer limit still isn't adjustable, and 10 minutes may not be enough for some users.
distractors.2: Contacting support is not a simple action within the content, and the user would likely be logged out while trying.

sources.title: Understanding SC 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable
sources.note: The turn off, adjust and extend options, and the exceptions.

question: A keyboard user must press Tab more than 40 times on every page to get past the site navigation. Which technique addresses WCAG 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks?
options: Adding a "Skip to main content" link at the top of each page
Making each navigation link larger and easier to click
Increasing the color contrast of the navigation links
Adding a site map page linked from the page footer
rationale: Success criterion 2.4.1 (Level A) requires a way to bypass blocks of content that repeat across pages, such as headers and navigation. Sufficient techniques include a skip link to the main content, headings at the start of each section, and ARIA landmarks. It helps anyone who moves through a page in sequence: keyboard users, screen reader users, switch users and people using screen magnifiers.

distractors.1: Larger links help people with motor impairments hit them, but they still have to tab through every one.
distractors.2: Better contrast helps people read the navigation, not skip it.
distractors.3: A site map helps people find pages, but on each page they would still have to tab through the repeated navigation.

sources.title: Understanding SC 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks
sources.note: Intent and techniques: skip links, headings and landmarks.

question: A design team removes the browser's focus outline because they find it unattractive and doesn't replace it. Which users are most directly affected?
options: Blind users who navigate with a screen reader
Deaf users who rely on captions
Sighted people who navigate by keyboard
Mouse users who have hand tremors
rationale: Success criterion 2.4.7 Focus Visible (Level AA) requires a visible indicator of keyboard focus. Without it, sighted people who navigate by keyboard, including many people with motor disabilities, can't tell where they are or what pressing Enter will do. It also helps people with attention or memory limitations. Custom focus styles are fine, as long as they are clearly visible.

distractors.0: Screen readers announce the focused element, so blind users don't depend on the visual outline. Sighted keyboard users do.
distractors.1: Deafness doesn't affect seeing focus.
distractors.3: Mouse users point directly at what they want, so they rely much less on a focus indicator.

sources.title: Understanding SC 2.4.7 Focus Visible
sources.note: Intent and who benefits.

question: As a keyboard user tabs down a page, a sticky cookie banner completely covers the focused link. Which WCAG 2.2 success criterion does this fail?
options: 2.4.3 Focus Order
2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)
1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus
3.2.1 On Focus
rationale: Success criterion 2.4.11 (Level AA, added in WCAG 2.2) requires that a focused component is not entirely hidden by content the author created, such as sticky headers, footers or cookie banners. At AA, partial overlap is allowed; the AAA version, 2.4.12, requires the item to be fully visible. Fixes include scroll padding so focused items scroll clear of sticky elements, or making the banner modal so it is dismissed first.

distractors.0: Focus Order is about whether focus moves in a logical sequence. Here the order may be fine; the problem is that the focused item can't be seen.
distractors.2: Content on Hover or Focus covers extra content that appears when hovering or focusing, such as tooltips. A cookie banner isn't triggered by focus.
distractors.3: On Focus is about receiving focus causing an unexpected change of context.

sources.title: Understanding SC 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)
sources.note: Intent, sticky headers and cookie banners, and sufficient techniques.

question: WCAG 2.2 introduced 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) at Level AA. What minimum size does it set for pointer targets, unless an exception applies?
options: 16 by 16 CSS pixels
44 by 44 CSS pixels
48 by 48 CSS pixels
24 by 24 CSS pixels
rationale: Success criterion 2.5.8 requires pointer targets to be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels. Smaller targets can still pass if they have enough spacing, if an equivalent control meets the size, if they sit inline in text, if their size is essential or legally required, or if the browser controls the size. Bigger targets help people with tremors or limited dexterity, and anyone using a phone on the move.

distractors.0: 16 by 16 is smaller than the AA minimum.
distractors.1: 44 by 44 is the Level AAA requirement in 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), and a common platform guideline, but not the AA minimum.
distractors.2: 48 by 48 is a common platform design recommendation, not a WCAG number.

tip: AA: 24 by 24. AAA: 44 by 44.

sources.title: Understanding SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)
sources.note: The 24 by 24 minimum and its exceptions.

question: A French-language website doesn't declare its language in the code, and screen readers read it with English pronunciation. Which WCAG success criterion is failed?
options: 3.1.1 Language of Page
3.1.5 Reading Level
1.3.1 Info and Relationships
4.1.2 Name, Role, Value
rationale: Success criterion 3.1.1 (Level A) requires that the default human language of each page can be determined by software. In HTML that is the lang attribute on the html element, for example lang="fr". Screen readers and text-to-speech tools use it to choose the right pronunciation rules. It also helps tools such as translation and captioning. A related criterion, 3.1.2 Language of Parts, covers passages in a different language.

distractors.1: Reading Level (AAA) is about how difficult the text is to read, not which language it is in.
distractors.2: Info and Relationships is about structure such as headings and labels.
distractors.3: Name, Role, Value is about interface controls exposing their information to assistive technology.

sources.title: Understanding SC 3.1.1 Language of Page
sources.note: Intent, who benefits, and the lang attribute technique.

question: Choosing a country from a dropdown immediately loads a different page, without warning and without a submit button. Which WCAG success criterion addresses this?
options: 2.1.1 Keyboard
3.3.2 Labels or Instructions
3.2.2 On Input
2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context)
rationale: Success criterion 3.2.2 (Level A) says that changing a setting in a form control should not cause an unexpected change of context unless the user was told beforehand. Loading a new page, opening a window or moving focus as soon as an option is chosen is disorienting, especially for screen reader users, people with low vision and people with cognitive disabilities. Keyboard users can also trigger it by accident while arrowing through options. A separate Go or Submit button fixes it.

distractors.0: The dropdown may be fully keyboard operable. The problem is the unexpected change, not keyboard access.
distractors.1: Labels or Instructions is about telling users what input is expected. It doesn't cover controls that change context on their own.
distractors.3: Link Purpose is about understanding where links go. A dropdown is a form control, not a link.

tip: 3.2.x criteria are about predictability: nothing big should happen just because something received focus (3.2.1) or a value changed (3.2.2).

sources.title: Understanding SC 3.2.2 On Input
sources.note: Intent and failures for unexpected changes of context.

question: When a form submission fails, the only sign is a red border around the invalid field. What does WCAG 3.3.1 Error Identification require?
options: Play a warning sound whenever an error is detected
Clear the form so the user can start again from scratch
Make the red border at least 3 pixels wide so it stands out
Identify the field in error and describe the error in text
rationale: Success criterion 3.3.1 (Level A) requires that when an input error is detected automatically, the field in error is identified and the error is described in text. Color, icons or borders can support the message, but text is required, so screen reader users and people who can't see the color difference get it too. The message can appear inline, in a summary at the top, or both. Related criteria go further: 3.3.3 asks for suggestions to fix the error.

distractors.0: A sound is not a text description, and many users won't hear it or know what it means.
distractors.1: Clearing the form makes errors harder to fix and doesn't identify anything.
distractors.2: A thicker border is still a visual-only cue.

sources.title: Understanding SC 3.3.1 Error Identification
sources.note: Intent and techniques for identifying and describing errors.

question: A login page blocks pasting into the password field, so password managers can't fill it. Which WCAG 2.2 success criterion does this affect most directly?
options: 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum)
3.3.7 Redundant Entry
1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose
2.2.1 Timing Adjustable
rationale: Success criterion 3.3.8 (Level AA) says no step in a login process may require a cognitive function test, such as remembering a password or transcribing a code, unless an alternative or a supporting mechanism is available. Password managers and copy and paste are the mechanisms that make passwords acceptable, so blocking them fails. Object recognition and identifying your own uploaded content are allowed at AA. It mainly helps people with memory, reading or other cognitive disabilities.

distractors.1: Redundant Entry is about not asking users to re-enter information they already gave in the same process. It doesn't cover login tests.
distractors.2: Identify Input Purpose helps browsers autofill personal data fields. It supports the same goal but isn't the criterion that bans blocking paste in authentication.
distractors.3: Timing Adjustable is about time limits, not how users prove who they are.

sources.title: Understanding SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum)
sources.note: What counts as a cognitive function test and the permitted alternatives.

question: A developer builds a custom toggle from a styled div with a click handler. Screen readers announce nothing useful about it. Which WCAG success criterion does this fail?
options: 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)
2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)
4.1.2 Name, Role, Value
3.1.1 Language of Page
rationale: Success criterion 4.1.2 (Level A) requires every interface component to expose its name, role and current state to assistive technology, and to let it be operated. Native HTML controls do this automatically. A scripted div doesn't, so a screen reader can't tell the user it is a toggle, what it controls, or whether it is on. The fix is to use a native element such as a button, or add the right WAI-ARIA role, state and accessible name.

distractors.0: Contrast is about visibility, not what assistive technology can detect.
distractors.1: Target size is about how easy a control is to hit with a pointer.
distractors.3: Language of Page is about pronunciation, not controls.

tip: Native HTML first. If a custom control is unavoidable, ARIA must supply the name, role and state.

sources.title: Understanding SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value
sources.note: Intent for custom controls and related ARIA techniques and failures.

question: A team meets a WCAG success criterion using a method that isn't in W3C's list of sufficient techniques. Can the content still conform?
options: No, because only W3C-listed sufficient techniques count
Only if W3C reviews and approves the alternative method
Only for Level A criteria, not for Level AA criteria
Yes, because techniques are informative, not required
rationale: In WCAG, the success criteria are the normative requirements: conformance is judged against them. The techniques documents are informative guidance showing known ways to meet a criterion. Content doesn't have to use W3C's published techniques. Any method that actually satisfies the criterion counts, and failing one technique's test doesn't by itself mean failing WCAG. This lets WCAG stay technology-neutral while technology changes.

distractors.0: W3C says outright that techniques are not required.
distractors.1: W3C doesn't approve or certify individual implementations.
distractors.2: The normative and informative distinction applies at every level.

tip: Normative = required (the success criteria). Informative = helpful guidance (Understanding documents and techniques).

sources.title: Understanding Techniques for WCAG Success Criteria
sources.note: Explains that techniques are informative and other methods can meet the criteria.

question: Under the 2010 ADA Standards, what is the minimum clear floor space needed in front of an element such as a drinking fountain or a control, to fit a single stationary wheelchair?
options: 24 by 36 inches
30 by 48 inches
36 by 60 inches
48 by 48 inches
rationale: Section 305 sets the minimum clear floor or ground space at 30 by 48 inches, for either a forward or a side approach. The space must be level, firm and free of obstructions so a wheelchair user can pull up to the element. Where a forward approach is required, such as at a lavatory, knee and toe clearance underneath is also needed. Turning space, used to change direction, is a separate and larger requirement.

distractors.0: 24 by 36 inches is too small to hold a typical wheelchair.
distractors.2: 36 by 60 inches is larger than the minimum. 36 inches is the minimum accessible route width, and 60 inches is the turning circle diameter.
distractors.3: 48 by 48 inches is not the clear floor space dimension in the Standards.

sources.title: U.S. Access Board: Guide to the ADA Standards, Clear Floor or Ground Space and Turning Space
sources.note: Sections 304 and 305, with diagrams.

question: A wheelchair user needs to turn around in an accessible restroom. Which turning space does the 2010 ADA Standards allow?
options: A circle at least 48 inches across
A 60-inch circle, or a T-shaped space
A square measuring 36 by 36 inches
Any space at least 30 inches wide
rationale: Section 304 allows two forms of turning space: a circle at least 60 inches across, or a T-shaped space within a 60-inch square, with arms and stem at least 36 inches wide. The T-shape lets the user make a three-point turn. Turning space can overlap clear floor spaces, and doors may swing into it. Without it, a wheelchair user can enter a room but not turn to use fixtures or leave forwards.

distractors.0: A 48-inch circle is too small for most wheelchairs to turn in.
distractors.2: 36 inches is the width of each arm of the T-shape, not a turning space by itself.
distractors.3: 30 inches is the width of a clear floor space, which holds a stationary wheelchair but doesn't allow turning.

sources.title: U.S. Access Board: Guide to the ADA Standards, Clear Floor or Ground Space and Turning Space
sources.note: Circular and T-shaped turning space, section 304.

question: Under the 2010 ADA Standards, what is the unobstructed forward or side reach range for operable parts such as light switches and card readers?
options: 10 to 40 inches above the floor
20 to 54 inches above the floor
15 to 48 inches above the floor
24 to 60 inches above the floor
rationale: Section 308 sets the unobstructed reach range at 15 to 48 inches above the floor for both forward and side reach. Reaching over an obstruction, such as a counter, lowers the maximum. The range covers only the parts someone has to operate, so the rest of an element can sit outside it. Placing controls within this range lets seated users, people of short stature and children use them.

distractors.0: 40 inches is lower than necessary, and 10 inches is too low to reach comfortably from a seat.
distractors.1: 54 inches is above the 48-inch maximum, so many seated users couldn't reach it.
distractors.3: 60 inches is out of reach for most seated users. It is the upper limit for tactile sign characters, not controls.

sources.title: U.S. Access Board: Guide to the ADA Standards, Operable Parts
sources.note: Reach ranges (section 308) and operation requirements (section 309).

question: Which door hardware is compliant under the 2010 ADA Standards?
options: A round knob that must be gripped tightly and turned
A thumb latch that must be pinched to release the door
A lever handle that works with one hand and no twisting
A keypad mounted 54 inches above the finished floor
rationale: Door hardware must work with one hand, without tight grasping, pinching or twisting of the wrist, and with no more than 5 pounds of force. It must be mounted 34 to 48 inches above the floor. Lever handles and U-shaped pulls meet this; round knobs don't. The same rules apply to other operable parts, which helps people with arthritis, limited grip strength or full hands.

distractors.0: Round knobs need tight grasping and twisting, so they don't comply.
distractors.1: Pinching is specifically ruled out.
distractors.3: 54 inches is above the 48-inch maximum for door hardware and reach ranges.

sources.title: U.S. Access Board: Guide to the ADA Standards, Entrances, Doors, and Gates
sources.note: Door hardware (section 404.2.7), clear width and maneuvering clearance.

question: What is the minimum clear width of an accessible doorway under the 2010 ADA Standards, measured with the door open 90 degrees?
options: 28 inches
30 inches
36 inches
32 inches
rationale: Doorways need at least 32 inches of clear width, measured from the face of the open door to the stop on the other side. It is measured as clear width, not as the size of the door leaf. Accessible routes are 36 inches wide but may narrow to 32 inches for up to 24 inches, which covers doorways. Doors also need level maneuvering space on both sides and thresholds no higher than half an inch.

distractors.0: 28 inches is too narrow for many wheelchairs.
distractors.1: 30 inches is the width of a clear floor space, not a doorway.
distractors.2: 36 inches is the minimum width of an accessible route. Doorways may be narrower, at 32 inches.

sources.title: U.S. Access Board: Guide to the ADA Standards, Entrances, Doors, and Gates
sources.note: Clear width (section 404.2.3) and other door requirements.

question: A wall-mounted fire extinguisher cabinet sticks 8 inches into a corridor, with its bottom edge 40 inches above the floor. Who does this mainly put at risk, and why?
options: Blind people who use a long cane, which sweeps below it
Wheelchair users, because it narrows the corridor below 36 inches
Deaf people, because they can't hear it as they approach
Tall people, because it sits at about chest or head height
rationale: Objects with leading edges between 27 and 80 inches high may protrude no more than 4 inches into a circulation path. A long cane sweeps close to the ground, so it detects objects below 27 inches, but anything higher and deeper than 4 inches can hit a blind person's body or head without warning. Circulation paths also need at least 80 inches of headroom. Fixes include recessing the cabinet or putting a cane-detectable barrier underneath.

distractors.1: Protruding objects can narrow a route, but the specific risk of a high, deep object is that canes can't detect it.
distractors.2: The risk is physical collision. Hearing doesn't affect it.
distractors.3: At 40 inches the object is below head height for nearly everyone. The danger is to people who can't see it.

sources.title: U.S. Access Board: Guide to the ADA Standards, Protruding Objects
sources.note: The 4-inch protrusion limit, the 27 to 80-inch zone, and headroom.

question: Under the 2010 ADA Standards, how many of a parking facility's accessible spaces must be van-accessible?
options: All of them
At least 1 in every 2
At least 1 in every 6
At least 1 in every 25
rationale: At least one of every six accessible spaces (or fraction of six) in each facility must be van-accessible. A van space can be 132 inches wide with a 60-inch access aisle, or 96 inches wide with a 96-inch aisle, and it needs a sign with the words "van accessible" in addition to the International Symbol of Accessibility. The designation is informational: anyone with an accessible parking permit may use it.

distractors.0: Requiring every space to be van-sized would take a lot of space without need. The Standards set a ratio.
distractors.1: 1 in 2 is much higher than the Standards require.
distractors.3: 1 in 25 is far fewer van spaces than the Standards require.

sources.title: U.S. Access Board: Guide to the ADA Standards, Parking Spaces
sources.note: Van-accessible ratio, space and aisle dimensions, and signage.

question: Why do accessible parking spaces need a marked access aisle beside them?
options: To give drivers of all cars extra room to open their doors
To give room to transfer to a wheelchair or deploy a van lift
To give shoppers a safe place to leave their shopping carts
To show where the accessible parking sign must be mounted
rationale: The access aisle, at least 60 inches wide and as long as the space, gives a wheelchair user room to get between the car and the chair, and room for a van's ramp or lift, usually on the passenger side. It must connect to the accessible route and be marked so people don't park in it. Curb ramps, posts and bollards can't intrude into it. A space without a clear aisle can be unusable even if it is signed as accessible.

distractors.0: Extra door room helps everyone, but the aisle's purpose is transfer and lift space for wheelchair users.
distractors.2: Using the aisle for storage would block the access it exists to provide.
distractors.3: Signs mark the space and must be at least 60 inches high, but that is not why the aisle exists.

sources.title: U.S. Access Board: Guide to the ADA Standards, Parking Spaces
sources.note: Access aisle requirements and why they matter.

question: Where should a tactile room identification sign with raised characters and braille be placed beside a single door, under the 2010 ADA Standards?
options: On the door itself, at the average adult's eye level
Above the door frame, where it can be seen from a distance
On the wall on the hinge side of the door, at any height
On the latch side wall, 48 to 60 inches above the floor
rationale: Permanent room identification signs, such as room numbers and restroom labels, need raised characters and braille. They go on the wall on the latch side of the door, with the baseline of the tactile characters between 48 and 60 inches above the floor. Consistent placement lets blind people find signs by touch without searching. There must also be clear floor space in front of the sign, outside the door's swing, so the reader isn't hit by the door.

distractors.0: Signs on a door move when it opens and are hard to find by touch. The Standards allow push-side placement only in limited cases.
distractors.1: Above the door is out of reach for reading by touch.
distractors.2: The hinge side is where a person reading the sign could be hit by the opening door. The Standards specify the latch side.

sources.title: U.S. Access Board: Guide to the ADA Standards, Signs
sources.note: Which signs need tactile characters, and mounting height and location.

question: Under the 2010 ADA Standards, what are the minimum clear width and maximum running slope of a walking surface on an accessible route?
options: 36 inches wide, running slope no steeper than 1:20
32 inches wide, running slope no steeper than 1:12
48 inches wide, running slope no steeper than 1:8
30 inches wide, no slope limit
rationale: An accessible route needs a continuous clear width of at least 36 inches, narrowing to 32 inches only for short stretches such as doorways. Its walking surfaces may be no steeper than 1:20 in the direction of travel and 1:48 across. Anything steeper than 1:20 must be built as a ramp, with handrails and landings. Accessible routes must link site arrival points, such as parking, transit stops and sidewalks, to accessible entrances and spaces.

distractors.1: 32 inches is allowed only for short stretches like doorways, and 1:12 is the maximum ramp slope, not a walking surface slope.
distractors.2: 1:8 is far too steep and is allowed only in very limited alteration cases.
distractors.3: 30 inches is a clear floor space dimension, and accessible routes do have slope limits.

sources.title: U.S. Access Board: Guide to the ADA Standards, Accessible Routes
sources.note: Width, running and cross slope, and what accessible routes must connect.

question: What is the purpose of detectable warnings, the surfaces of truncated domes at transit platform edges and some curb ramps?
options: To give wheelchair wheels better traction on wet slopes
To help rainwater drain off curb ramps and platforms
To warn blind pedestrians, by touch, of a street or drop-off
To mark the start of the accessible parking area
rationale: Detectable warnings are a standardized pattern of small flat-topped domes that can be felt underfoot or with a long cane. They signal the edge of a hazard, such as a street crossing or a rail platform drop-off. They are required at platform edges and at curb ramps in transit facilities and on federally funded street projects. Curb ramps remove the step for wheelchair users, but they also remove the curb that blind pedestrians used to detect the street, which is why the warning texture matters.

distractors.0: The domes exist to be felt, not to add traction for wheelchairs.
distractors.1: Drainage is handled by slope and grates. The dome pattern is for tactile detection.
distractors.3: Accessible parking is marked with signs and the International Symbol of Accessibility, not domes.

sources.title: U.S. Access Board: Guide to the ADA Standards, Ramps and Curb Ramps
sources.note: Detectable warnings and curb ramps, including where warnings are required.

question: Under the 2010 ADA Standards, how large a vertical change in level is allowed on an accessible route with no treatment at all?
options: Up to 1/4 inch
Up to 1 inch
Up to 2 inches
Up to 1/2 inch
rationale: Changes in level up to 1/4 inch may be vertical. Between 1/4 and 1/2 inch they must be beveled at no steeper than 1:2. Anything over 1/2 inch must be treated as a ramp or curb ramp. Small lips catch wheelchair casters and walker feet and cause trips, so these limits matter for everyone. Ground openings, such as grates, also must not let a 1/2-inch sphere through.

distractors.1: One inch is enough to stop a wheelchair caster and must be ramped.
distractors.2: Two inches is a step, not a small change in level.
distractors.3: Up to 1/2 inch is allowed only if beveled. Without treatment, the limit is 1/4 inch.

sources.title: U.S. Access Board: Guide to the ADA Standards, Floor and Ground Surfaces
sources.note: Firm, stable and slip-resistant surfaces, openings and changes in level.

question: A building's main entrance has steps, and wheelchair users must go around to a separate entrance by the loading dock. Which universal design principle does this most clearly violate?
options: Tolerance for Error
Equitable Use
Low Physical Effort
Simple and Intuitive Use
rationale: Equitable Use asks that a design be useful and appealing to people with diverse abilities. Its guidelines call for the same means of use for everyone, identical where possible and equivalent where not, and for avoiding segregating or stigmatizing any users. A back entrance by the loading dock technically provides access, but it separates wheelchair users from everyone else. A level main entrance that everyone shares would meet the principle.

distractors.0: Tolerance for Error is about reducing hazards and the effects of mistakes. The problem here is separation.
distractors.2: Low Physical Effort is about minimizing fatigue. The separate route may also be longer, but the core issue is segregation.
distractors.3: Simple and Intuitive Use is about being easy to understand. The issue isn't confusion but unequal treatment.

tip: If a scenario makes disabled people use a separate or second-class route, think Equitable Use.

sources.title: Centre for Excellence in Universal Design: The 7 Principles
sources.note: Each principle with its guidelines, including 1b, avoid segregating or stigmatizing users.

question: Scissors designed to work equally well in the left or right hand best illustrate which universal design principle?
options: Perceptible Information
Size and Space for Approach and Use
Flexibility in Use
Equitable Use
rationale: Flexibility in Use means the design accommodates a wide range of individual preferences and abilities. Its guidelines include offering a choice of methods, supporting both left- and right-handed use, helping users be accurate, and letting them work at their own pace. Ambidextrous scissors are the classic example. Digital examples include letting users choose between keyboard, mouse, touch and voice.

distractors.0: Perceptible Information is about communicating information through different senses and in different conditions.
distractors.1: Size and Space is about room to approach, reach and use something, whatever the user's body size or mobility.
distractors.3: Equitable Use is about the same or equivalent use for everyone without segregation. Handedness is specifically listed under Flexibility in Use.

sources.title: Centre for Excellence in Universal Design: The 7 Principles
sources.note: Principle 2 and its guidelines, including 2b, left- and right-handed use.

question: A ticket machine removes unnecessary menu steps, uses familiar icons with short labels, and confirms each step as it happens. Which universal design principle does this apply?
options: Simple and Intuitive Use
Low Physical Effort
Tolerance for Error
Flexibility in Use
rationale: Simple and Intuitive Use means a design is easy to understand regardless of the user's experience, knowledge, language skills or concentration. Its guidelines are to remove unnecessary complexity, match users' expectations, support a wide range of literacy and language skills, arrange information by importance, and give clear prompts and feedback. These choices help people with cognitive disabilities, tourists, first-time users and people in a hurry.

distractors.1: Low Physical Effort is about reducing fatigue and force, not mental effort.
distractors.2: Feedback can help avoid errors, but removing complexity and matching expectations are the core of Simple and Intuitive Use.
distractors.3: Flexibility in Use is about offering choices. This scenario is about making one path easy to understand.

sources.title: Centre for Excellence in Universal Design: The 7 Principles
sources.note: Principle 3 and its guidelines.

question: An elevator announces each floor aloud, shows it on a display, and has raised and braille floor buttons. Which universal design principle does this most directly apply?
options: Equitable Use
Low Physical Effort
Size and Space for Approach and Use
Perceptible Information
rationale: Perceptible Information means the design communicates necessary information effectively, whatever the surrounding conditions or the user's sensory abilities. Its first guideline is to present essential information in more than one mode: pictorial, verbal and tactile. Others call for good contrast, maximum legibility and compatibility with devices used by people with sensory impairments. The elevator gives the same information by sound, sight and touch.

distractors.0: Equitable Use is about everyone using the same means without segregation. The specific feature here is multiple sensory channels.
distractors.1: Low Physical Effort is about reducing force and fatigue.
distractors.2: Size and Space is about reach and room to maneuver, not how information is conveyed.

tip: WCAG's Perceivable principle echoes this one: offer information through more than one sense.

sources.title: Centre for Excellence in Universal Design: The 7 Principles
sources.note: Principle 4 and its guidelines, including 4a, multiple modes.

question: A product team replaces a stiff twist-off cap with a push-button opening that needs little force and no wrist rotation. Which universal design principle is this?
options: Low Physical Effort
Tolerance for Error
Simple and Intuitive Use
Perceptible Information
rationale: Low Physical Effort means the design can be used efficiently and comfortably with minimal fatigue. Its guidelines are to let users keep a neutral body position, use reasonable operating forces, minimize repetitive actions, and minimize sustained effort. A push button with low force helps people with arthritis or limited grip, older people, and anyone with their hands full. The ADA Standards apply the same idea to controls: no tight grasping or wrist twisting.

distractors.1: Tolerance for Error is about minimizing hazards and mistakes, not effort.
distractors.2: The change is about physical force, not understanding.
distractors.3: Nothing here changes how information is communicated.

sources.title: Centre for Excellence in Universal Design: The 7 Principles
sources.note: Principle 6 and its guidelines.

question: A service counter has a lowered section with knee clearance so seated customers can see the clerk and reach the card reader. Which universal design principle is this?
options: Flexibility in Use
Perceptible Information
Size and Space for Approach and Use
Simple and Intuitive Use
rationale: Size and Space for Approach and Use means providing enough size and space to approach, reach, manipulate and use a design, whatever the user's body size, posture or mobility. Its guidelines call for a clear line of sight and comfortable reach for both seated and standing users, room for different hand sizes, and space for assistive devices or a personal assistant. A lowered counter section works for wheelchair users, people of short stature and children.

distractors.0: A lowered section does offer an option, but sightlines and reach for seated users are named directly in Size and Space.
distractors.1: Perceptible Information is about communicating information through different senses.
distractors.3: The counter isn't about how easy something is to understand.

sources.title: Centre for Excellence in Universal Design: The 7 Principles
sources.note: Principle 7 and its guidelines.

question: Who developed the seven principles of universal design, and when?
options: Ronald Mace's working group at NC State University, in 1997
The World Wide Web Consortium, alongside WCAG 1.0 in 1999
The United Nations, as part of the CRPD adopted in 2006
CAST, as part of its Universal Design for Learning framework
rationale: The seven principles were developed in 1997 at North Carolina State University by a working group of architects, product designers, engineers and environmental design researchers, led by Ronald Mace. They apply to environments, products and communications. Later frameworks, such as UDL in education and inclusive design in technology, build on the same idea.

distractors.1: W3C published WCAG 1.0 in 1999. It is a web content standard, not the universal design principles.
distractors.2: The CRPD defines universal design and promotes it, but it didn't create the seven principles.
distractors.3: CAST created UDL, which adapts universal design to learning. The seven principles came first.

sources.title: Centre for Excellence in Universal Design: The 7 Principles
sources.note: The principles and the NCSU working group that developed them.

question: Which statement best describes universal design?
options: Adapting a product for a specific person after they request it
A separate product line made especially for disabled people
A legal code that sets minimum dimensions for buildings
Designing so as many people as possible can use it, unadapted
rationale: Universal design aims to make environments, products and services usable by as many people as possible, without needing adaptation or specialized design. Ireland's Centre for Excellence in Universal Design describes it as a basic condition of good design, not a special requirement that benefits only a minority. The CRPD's definition adds that universal design doesn't exclude assistive devices for particular groups where they are needed.

distractors.0: Adapting for a specific person on request describes an accommodation.
distractors.1: Separate products for disabled people are specialized design, the opposite of the universal approach.
distractors.2: Codes such as the ADA Standards set minimums. Universal design is a broader approach that aims beyond compliance.

sources.title: Centre for Excellence in Universal Design: About Universal Design
sources.note: Definition of universal design and why it is good design.

sources.title: UN CRPD Article 2: Definitions
sources.note: The CRPD definition of universal design.

question: Microsoft's inclusive design principle "Solve for one, extend to many" means what?
options: Design for the average user so that most people are served
Designing with disabled people yields solutions that help many
Build one product and then sell it in as many markets as possible
Fix accessibility issues one at a time, starting with the worst
rationale: Microsoft's inclusive design toolkit names three principles: recognize exclusion, learn from diversity, and solve for one, extend to many. The third says that designing for and with people who have permanent disabilities leads to solutions that help far more people, including those with temporary or situational limitations. It is the reasoning behind the curb-cut effect. Designing for an imagined average user tends to exclude people at the edges.

distractors.0: Designing for the average is the approach inclusive design argues against, because it excludes people whose needs differ.
distractors.2: The principle is about people, not markets.
distractors.3: The principle is about where designers look for insight, not how they schedule fixes.

sources.title: Microsoft Inclusive Design
sources.note: The three inclusive design principles.

question: According to Microsoft's inclusive design principles, where does exclusion most often come from?
options: From the impairments that people have
From strict accessibility laws and rules
From designers' own biases and assumptions
From products that have too many features
rationale: The first principle, recognize exclusion, says exclusion happens when designers solve problems using their own biases, so the experience doesn't match the people who need to use it. That places the problem in the design, not the person, which echoes the social model of disability. Recognizing exclusion is the first step: once a team sees who it is leaving out, it can learn from those people and design differently.

distractors.0: Locating the problem in impairments is the medical model. Inclusive design looks at mismatches the design creates.
distractors.1: Laws aim to reduce exclusion. They are not its source.
distractors.3: Complexity can cause problems, but the principle points to designers' assumptions as the root cause.

sources.title: Microsoft Inclusive Design
sources.note: Recognize exclusion, learn from diversity, solve for one and extend to many.

question: An employee with low vision asks for a specific large monitor. The employer offers a different setup that is equally effective and cheaper. Under EEOC guidance on the ADA, is that allowed?
options: No, the employer must provide exactly what the employee asks for
Yes, if it is equally effective; the employer chooses among effective options
Only if the employee agrees to the alternative in writing first
No, because cost can never be considered for an accommodation
rationale: Under EEOC guidance, the employee's preference should get primary consideration, but the employer has the final say between accommodations that are effective. It may choose the cheaper or easier option if it works just as well. The key test is effectiveness: an option that doesn't let the person do the job, or enjoy equal benefits of employment, doesn't count. Talking it through with the employee helps find the right fit.

distractors.0: The employee's preference matters, but it doesn't bind the employer if another option is equally effective.
distractors.2: Written agreement isn't a requirement for choosing among effective options.
distractors.3: Cost can be considered when choosing among effective options, and in deciding whether something is an undue hardship.

sources.title: EEOC: Enforcement Guidance on Reasonable Accommodation and Undue Hardship under the ADA
sources.note: Choosing among effective accommodations and the role of the employee's preference.

question: An employee tells a manager, "I'm having trouble getting to work at 8 because of my medical treatment." Under EEOC guidance, does this count as a request for reasonable accommodation?
options: No, because the employee didn't mention the ADA
No, because a request only counts if it is in writing
Yes, a request can be made in plain, everyday language
Only if the employee's doctor submits the request
rationale: EEOC guidance says people can ask for an accommodation in plain words, in conversation or any other way. They don't need to mention the ADA or use the phrase "reasonable accommodation". Once the employer knows the person needs a change at work for a reason related to a medical condition, it should start the interactive process. An employer may ask for a form to be completed later, but it can't ignore a spoken request.

distractors.0: No magic words are needed. Mentioning the ADA is not required.
distractors.1: An employer may ask for a written follow-up, but a spoken request still counts.
distractors.3: The employer may sometimes ask for documentation, but the request itself can come from the employee.

sources.title: EEOC: Enforcement Guidance on Reasonable Accommodation and Undue Hardship under the ADA
sources.note: How requests can be made and what happens next.

question: How does EEOC guidance describe "undue hardship" under the ADA?
options: Any accommodation that costs the employer money
Any change that coworkers or customers dislike
A fixed dollar limit written into the law itself
Significant difficulty or expense for that employer
rationale: Undue hardship means an accommodation would cause significant difficulty or expense for that particular employer. It is judged case by case, weighing the cost and impact against the employer's size, resources and operations. It also covers changes that would be unduly disruptive or would fundamentally change how the business operates. A large company will usually have a harder time showing undue hardship than a small one for the same accommodation.

distractors.0: Some cost is expected. Only significant difficulty or expense qualifies.
distractors.1: Coworker or customer preferences don't make an accommodation an undue hardship.
distractors.2: There is no fixed dollar threshold. It depends on the employer's circumstances.

sources.title: EEOC: Enforcement Guidance on Reasonable Accommodation and Undue Hardship under the ADA
sources.note: Definition and factors for undue hardship.

question: Under EEOC guidance, which of these falls outside an employer's reasonable accommodation obligations?
options: Removing an essential job function or lowering a standard
Changing the employee's work schedule or hours
Providing a sign language interpreter for a meeting
Modifying equipment or buying adapted equipment
rationale: Reasonable accommodation is about helping a qualified person do the job, not changing what the job is. Employers don't have to remove essential functions or lower production standards that apply to everyone, though they may choose to. They do have to consider accommodations that help the person meet those standards, such as modified schedules, adapted equipment, interpreters, job restructuring of marginal tasks, or reassignment to a vacant position.

distractors.1: Modified or part-time schedules are listed as possible reasonable accommodations.
distractors.2: Qualified readers and interpreters are listed as possible reasonable accommodations.
distractors.3: Acquiring or modifying equipment is a common reasonable accommodation.

sources.title: EEOC: Enforcement Guidance on Reasonable Accommodation and Undue Hardship under the ADA
sources.note: Types of accommodation and what employers don't have to do.

question: A Deaf applicant asks for a sign language interpreter at a job interview. Which category of reasonable accommodation is this?
options: A change to how essential job functions are performed
A change that provides equal benefits and privileges of employment
A change to the job application process
A personal-use item
rationale: EEOC guidance describes three categories of reasonable accommodation: changes to the application process so a qualified applicant can be considered; changes to the work environment or how a job is usually done, so the person can perform essential functions; and changes that give equal access to the benefits and privileges of employment, such as training or break rooms. An interpreter at an interview falls into the first category. Accommodation duties start before someone is hired.

distractors.0: The applicant isn't doing the job yet. This is about being able to apply and be considered.
distractors.1: Benefits and privileges cover things like training, events and facilities for current employees.
distractors.3: Personal-use items, such as hearing aids, are things a person needs on and off the job. Employers generally don't have to provide them.

sources.title: EEOC: Enforcement Guidance on Reasonable Accommodation and Undue Hardship under the ADA
sources.note: The three categories of reasonable accommodation.

question: An employee asks their employer to buy them a new personal wheelchair that they use everywhere, not just at work. Under EEOC guidance, is the employer generally required to provide it?
options: Yes, all disability-related equipment is a reasonable accommodation
No, personal-use items needed both on and off the job generally aren't required
Yes, if the employer has more than 15 employees
No, because wheelchairs are covered by Title III
rationale: EEOC guidance says employers generally don't have to provide personal-use items, such as wheelchairs, prosthetic limbs, eyeglasses or hearing aids, when the person also needs them away from work. The exception is when an item is designed for or needed to meet job-related needs rather than personal ones. Employers do have to consider workplace changes, such as accessible workstations, that let the person do the job with their own equipment.

distractors.0: Personal-use items are a recognized exception.
distractors.2: Fifteen employees is the threshold for Title I coverage. It doesn't change the personal-use rule.
distractors.3: Title III covers businesses open to the public. It doesn't provide personal mobility devices.

sources.title: EEOC: Enforcement Guidance on Reasonable Accommodation and Undue Hardship under the ADA
sources.note: Personal-use items and when they are or aren't required.

question: According to the CRPD's definition, how does universal design relate to assistive devices?
options: Universal design removes the need for all assistive devices
Universal design and assistive devices can't be used together
Universal design is itself a type of assistive device
Universal design still allows assistive devices where needed
rationale: The CRPD defines universal design as designing products, environments, programs and services to be usable by everyone to the greatest extent possible, without adaptation or specialized design. It then adds that this does not exclude assistive devices for particular groups where needed. Universal design reduces how often individual solutions are required, but some people will always need assistive technology or accommodations. The two approaches work together.

distractors.0: The CRPD explicitly says universal design doesn't exclude assistive devices. No design meets every need.
distractors.1: Good universal design is compatible with assistive technology. Accessible websites work with screen readers, for example.
distractors.2: Assistive devices are tools for individuals. Universal design is an approach to designing for everyone.

sources.title: UN CRPD Article 2: Definitions
sources.note: Definitions of universal design and reasonable accommodation.

question: Company A captions every training video when it is produced. Company B adds captions only when a Deaf employee asks for a specific video. Which statement is most accurate?
options: A is universal design; B is accommodation on request
Both companies are taking a universal design approach
Both companies are providing individual accommodations
B is more efficient, because it captions only what's needed
rationale: Building captions into production is a universal design approach: access is there from the start for anyone, including people who are hard of hearing, non-native speakers and people in noisy or quiet places. Captioning on request is an accommodation: it responds to one person's need after it comes up, and the person waits. W3C notes that building accessibility in from the start is more efficient than retrofitting it. Accommodations are still needed for needs that design can't anticipate.

distractors.1: Company B's approach depends on an individual request, which is the hallmark of an accommodation.
distractors.2: Company A captions everything up front for all users, which is a design approach, not an individual accommodation.
distractors.3: Reactive captioning creates delays for the person who asked and often costs more over time than building it in.
