sources.note: Who benefits from accessibility, and why building it in early is more efficient.

sources.title: UN CRPD Article 2: Definitions
sources.note: Definitions of universal design and reasonable accommodation.

question: What does the Job Accommodation Network (JAN) describe as the "interactive process"?
options: A formal hearing that decides whether someone is disabled
A collaborative conversation to find an effective accommodation
An online form that automatically approves every request
A government process for reporting discrimination at work
rationale: The interactive process is a collaborative, often informal conversation between an employer and an employee with a disability. Together they identify the specific limitation and barrier, look at options, consider the employee's preference along with effectiveness and cost, choose an accommodation, and check whether it works. It is case by case because accommodations are individual. JAN is a free service that advises employers and employees on accommodations.

distractors.0: The interactive process is problem solving, not a hearing.
distractors.2: Accommodations are individualized and need discussion; they can't be approved automatically.
distractors.3: Complaints go to agencies such as the EEOC. The interactive process happens within the workplace.

sources.title: Job Accommodation Network: The Interactive Process
sources.note: Steps and tips for the interactive process.

question: A W3C case study reports that after a radio show added transcripts to its whole archive, search traffic and unique visitors rose. Which benefit of accessibility does this mainly show?
options: Reduced legal risk from regulators
Lower costs for hosting audio files
Wider market reach and discoverability
Faster page loads for every visitor
rationale: In the W3C business case, This American Life added transcripts after new FCC rules and saw search traffic rise by about 7% and unique visitors by about 4%. Search engines can index text but not audio, and transcripts also helped non-native English speakers and people in noisy places. Accessibility features often expand an audience beyond disabled users, which is part of the market reach argument.

distractors.0: Meeting regulations can reduce legal risk, but the case study's results are about traffic and audience.
distractors.1: Adding transcripts doesn't reduce hosting costs.
distractors.3: Transcripts don't make pages load faster.

sources.title: W3C WAI: The Business Case for Digital Accessibility
sources.note: Case study on transcripts, search traffic and wider audiences.

question: The 2008 settlement between the National Federation of the Blind and Target over an inaccessible website is most often cited as an example of which benefit of accessibility?
options: Minimizing legal risk
Driving innovation
Enhancing brand
Improving search rankings
rationale: The NFB sued Target because blind shoppers couldn't use its website. The 2008 settlement included about $6 million in class damages, more than $3 million in the plaintiffs' legal fees, and years of court oversight of the website. W3C's business case uses it to show the cost of ignoring accessibility, alongside other legal developments such as the Winn-Dixie case and accessibility laws in Europe. Avoiding that cost is one of the four business benefits.

distractors.1: Innovation refers to accessibility features becoming useful to everyone, such as voice control.
distractors.2: Brand benefits come from being seen as inclusive and socially responsible. A lawsuit tends to hurt a brand.
distractors.3: Accessible markup can help search, but the Target case is about legal exposure.

sources.title: W3C WAI: The Business Case for Digital Accessibility
sources.note: Minimize Legal Risk section, including the Target settlement.

question: Strong text contrast helps people with low vision. Which other group does W3C give as benefiting from it?
options: People using a screen reader
People using a phone in bright sunlight
People who are Deaf
People using voice control
rationale: W3C points out that accessibility often helps people in situational limitations. High contrast helps anyone reading a screen in glare. Captions help people in noisy places or where they can't play sound. These overlaps are why accessibility and usability are closely connected, and why accessible design improves the experience for a much larger group than people with disabilities alone.

distractors.0: Screen reader users hear the content, so visual contrast doesn't affect them.
distractors.2: Contrast is a visual feature. Deaf users benefit from captions and transcripts.
distractors.3: Voice control is an input method. Contrast affects reading.

sources.title: W3C WAI: Introduction to Web Accessibility
sources.note: Accessibility benefits for people with situational limitations and others.

sources.title: W3C WAI: Accessibility, Usability, and Inclusion
sources.note: Examples of accessibility features that help everyone in limiting situations.

question: Why does designing to WCAG also benefit older people, according to W3C?
options: WCAG has a special section for people over 65
Most older people use screen readers to browse
Age-related changes overlap with needs WCAG covers
It doesn't; older people need separate guidelines
rationale: As people age, many experience reduced contrast sensitivity, difficulty hearing high frequencies, less fine motor control and changes in short-term memory and concentration. These overlap with the needs of people with disabilities, so W3C says its existing standards, including WCAG, address most of them. With populations ageing, accessibility serves a large and growing group, many of whom wouldn't describe themselves as disabled.

distractors.0: WCAG has no age-specific section. Its criteria address functional needs, whatever the cause.
distractors.1: Most older people with vision changes have low vision rather than blindness. They benefit more from contrast, text size and simple navigation.
distractors.3: W3C says the existing standards already cover most older users' needs.

sources.title: W3C WAI: Older Users and Web Accessibility
sources.note: Age-related changes and how WCAG addresses them.

question: According to W3C, why is it better to include accessibility from the start of a project?
options: Because laws only apply to new projects
Because it is more efficient than retrofitting accessibility later
Because accessibility can't be added once a site is live
Because users with disabilities only visit new sites
rationale: W3C says that building accessibility into a project from the beginning is more efficient than going back to fix it later. Retrofitting often means redesigning components, rewriting code and retesting. The CRPD makes the same point for ICT, calling for accessible design at an early stage so accessibility costs as little as possible. Early involvement of users with disabilities also catches problems when they are cheapest to fix.

distractors.0: Accessibility laws generally apply to existing sites and services too.
distractors.2: Accessibility can be added later; it is just usually more costly and disruptive.
distractors.3: People with disabilities use all kinds of sites, old and new.

sources.title: W3C WAI: Introduction to Web Accessibility
sources.note: Why building accessibility in from the start is more efficient.

sources.title: UN CRPD Article 9: Accessibility
sources.note: Promotes accessible ICT design at an early stage so costs stay low.

question: In the UK, what is the spending power of disabled people and their households often called?
options: The Silver Economy
The Pink Pound
The Green Dollar
The Purple Pound
rationale: The Purple Pound refers to the spending power of disabled people and their households in the UK. W3C's business case cites estimates of at least £249 billion a year. The point for businesses is that inaccessible products and services turn away a large market, and that people who can't use a service tend to take their money elsewhere. Similar figures are cited globally, where the disability market is estimated in the trillions of dollars.

distractors.0: The Silver Economy refers to the spending of older people. It overlaps with disability but isn't the same term.
distractors.1: The Pink Pound refers to the spending power of LGBTQ+ consumers.
distractors.2: The Green Dollar isn't a term for disabled consumers' spending.

sources.title: W3C WAI: The Business Case for Digital Accessibility
sources.note: Increase Market Reach section, including the Purple Pound estimate.

question: A bank makes accessibility an organization-wide strategy, aiming to be the most inclusive company in its index, and reports benefits to culture and customer loyalty. Which business benefit does this best illustrate?
options: Enhancing the brand
Minimizing legal risk
Driving innovation
Reducing hosting costs
rationale: W3C's business case includes Barclays as an example of accessibility as part of corporate social responsibility. Going beyond compliance can strengthen brand image, customer loyalty and workforce diversity, and show that an organization's values are real. Brand is one of four benefit areas in W3C's business case, along with innovation, market reach and legal risk.

distractors.1: Going beyond compliance also lowers legal risk, but the scenario is about reputation and culture.
distractors.2: Innovation is about accessibility features becoming mainstream features. The scenario is about strategy and reputation.
distractors.3: Hosting costs aren't part of the case.

sources.title: W3C WAI: The Business Case for Digital Accessibility
sources.note: Enhance Your Brand section and the Barclays case study.

question: Beyond people with disabilities, which of these groups does W3C name as benefiting from web accessibility?
options: Advertisers buying placements on search engines
People with slow or expensive internet connections
Developers who prefer one particular coding framework
Companies that host websites on their own servers
rationale: W3C lists several groups who benefit from accessibility beyond people with disabilities: people using phones and other small devices, older people, people with temporary disabilities such as a broken arm, people in situational limitations such as bright sunlight, and people with slow or costly internet. Text alternatives and well-structured pages, for example, still work when images or media don't load. This broad benefit is a key argument for accessibility.

distractors.0: Advertisers aren't among the groups W3C lists. Its list is about people using the web in different conditions.
distractors.2: Choice of framework has nothing to do with who benefits from accessible content.
distractors.3: Where a site is hosted doesn't make a group of users benefit from accessibility.

sources.title: W3C WAI: Introduction to Web Accessibility
sources.note: Groups who benefit from accessibility.

question: Making a page reflow to a single column for people who zoom in also helps which other group most directly?
options: Screen reader users
Phone and other small-screen users
Users of braille displays
People who are Deaf
rationale: Reflow lets content fit a narrow width without scrolling in two directions. That supports people with low vision who zoom in, and the same responsive layout serves phone users. W3C names mobile users among the groups who benefit from accessible design. Many accessibility requirements overlap with good mobile design, so an accessible site often works better on all devices.

distractors.0: Screen readers read content in sequence, so layout width matters much less to their users.
distractors.2: Braille display users read text in sequence; page width doesn't affect them.
distractors.3: Reflow is a visual layout feature; it doesn't involve audio.

sources.title: W3C WAI: Introduction to Web Accessibility
sources.note: Mobile users among the groups who benefit.

sources.note: Who benefits from reflow, including small-screen users.

question: A teacher lets students choose their own project topic and connects lessons to issues in their community. Which UDL principle does this apply?
options: Representation
Action & Expression
Engagement
Perceptible Information
rationale: Engagement addresses the why of learning: what motivates learners and keeps them going. Its guidelines in UDL 3.0 cover welcoming interests and identities (including choice and autonomy, and relevance), sustaining effort and persistence, and emotional capacity. Offering choice and connecting learning to students' lives are typical Engagement strategies. Learners differ in what motivates them, so several options work better than one.

distractors.0: Representation is about presenting content in several forms, such as text, audio and diagrams.
distractors.1: Action & Expression is about how learners show what they know and how they plan.
distractors.3: Perceptible Information is a principle of universal design, not UDL.

sources.title: CAST: Engagement
sources.note: Guidelines 7, 8 and 9 of the UDL Guidelines 3.0.

question: A course lets students show what they learned through an essay, a recorded presentation or a diagram, and allows speech-to-text. Which UDL principle is this?
options: Action & Expression
Engagement
Representation
Tolerance for Error
rationale: Action & Expression addresses the how of learning: how learners move through the environment, use tools, and show what they know. Its guidelines cover interaction (including access to assistive technologies), expression and communication (multiple media and tools), and strategy development, which supports executive functions such as setting goals and monitoring progress. Letting students choose how to show their learning, and supporting assistive tools, are core examples.

distractors.1: Engagement is about motivation and interest, not how learners demonstrate understanding.
distractors.2: Representation varies how content is presented to learners. Here, learners vary how they respond.
distractors.3: Tolerance for Error is a universal design principle about reducing hazards and mistakes.

sources.title: CAST: Action & Expression
sources.note: Guidelines 4, 5 and 6 of the UDL Guidelines 3.0.

question: A college course provides checklists, goal-setting templates and progress check-ins to help students plan long assignments. Under UDL 3.0, which guideline does this support?
options: Design Options for Perception
Design Options for Strategy Development
Design Options for Language & Symbols
Design Options for Emotional Capacity
rationale: Guideline 6, Strategy Development, falls under Action & Expression and supports executive functions. Its considerations include setting meaningful goals, anticipating and planning for challenges, organizing information and resources, and monitoring progress. Checklists, templates and check-ins scaffold these skills, which helps students with ADHD and other learning disabilities and many others.

distractors.0: Perception (Guideline 1) is about offering information in ways learners can perceive, such as captions or adjustable text.
distractors.2: Language & Symbols (Guideline 2) is about clarifying vocabulary, notation and language.
distractors.3: Emotional Capacity (Guideline 9) is about managing emotions, self-awareness and reflection.

sources.title: CAST: Action & Expression
sources.note: Guideline 6, Strategy Development, and its considerations.

question: ISO 9241-11 defines usability as the extent to which specified users can achieve specified goals in a specified context of use with which three qualities?
options: Speed, accuracy and appearance
Perceivable, operable and understandable
Learnability, memorability and errors
Effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction
rationale: ISO 9241-11 defines usability by effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction for specified users, goals and contexts. W3C notes that this definition covers accessibility only when the specified users include people with disabilities and the context includes assistive technologies. In practice, usability work often leaves disabled people out, which is why accessibility needs its own attention.

distractors.0: These aren't the terms of the ISO definition.
distractors.1: These are three of WCAG's four principles, not the ISO usability definition.
distractors.2: These are components of usability popularized by Jakob Nielsen, not the ISO 9241-11 definition.

sources.title: W3C WAI: Accessibility, Usability, and Inclusion
sources.note: How accessibility, usability and inclusion relate, including the ISO 9241-11 definition.

question: According to W3C, how do accessibility and usability relate?
options: They overlap, but accessibility adds technical requirements
They are two names for exactly the same thing
They are separate fields with nothing in common
Usability is a smaller subset of accessibility
rationale: W3C describes accessibility as making sure people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate and interact equally, and usability as designing products that work well for users. Much good accessibility practice, such as clear instructions and good contrast, is also good usability. But accessibility includes technical requirements, such as working with assistive technology, and usability research often doesn't include disabled people. Inclusion, sometimes called universal design, is the broadest of the three.

distractors.1: W3C treats them as related but distinct.
distractors.2: W3C stresses how much they overlap.
distractors.3: Neither is a subset of the other. Each covers things the other doesn't.

sources.title: W3C WAI: Accessibility, Usability, and Inclusion
sources.note: Definitions and how the three relate.

question: A team's site passes a full WCAG conformance review. According to W3C, why should they still test with users with disabilities?
options: Because conformance reviews are usually inaccurate
Because user testing can replace the conformance review
Because users reveal problems conformance checks miss
Because WCAG requires user testing for conformance
rationale: W3C says that conformance checks are important but don't show how a site actually works for people. Testing with disabled and older users uncovers usability issues that a conformance review misses. The reverse also holds: user testing alone can't determine whether a site is accessible. The two should be combined, ideally with informal checks throughout development rather than one formal test at the end.

distractors.0: Conformance reviews are valuable; they just don't cover everything.
distractors.1: W3C says user testing can't replace conformance evaluation.
distractors.3: WCAG conformance is judged against the success criteria. User testing is recommended practice, not a conformance requirement.

sources.title: W3C WAI: Involving Users in Evaluating Web Accessibility
sources.note: Why to involve users, and how it complements conformance evaluation.

question: A team is recruiting screen reader users to test a public benefits website that many first-time users will visit. Whom should they recruit, according to W3C?
options: Only expert screen reader users, to get the most efficient feedback
Only colleagues, to keep it confidential
Only people without disabilities using a screen reader for the first time
Participants who match the site's audience, including novice assistive technology users
rationale: W3C recommends matching participants to the people who will actually use the product. A public benefits site serves many inexperienced users, so novice assistive technology users should be included; an internal tool for experienced staff calls for advanced users. Include a few people with different disabilities and, where relevant, older users, and don't assume one person's experience represents everyone with the same disability.

distractors.0: Experts can work around problems that would stop novices, so they may miss real barriers on a public site.
distractors.2: People simulating a disability don't use assistive technology the way regular users do, so their results can be misleading.
distractors.1: Colleagues rarely match the real audience or its range of skills.

sources.title: W3C WAI: Involving Users in Evaluating Web Accessibility
sources.note: Recruiting participants who match the audience.

question: After testing with three participants with disabilities, how should a team report its findings, according to W3C?
options: As statistically proven results for all disabled users
As evidence that the site conforms to WCAG 2.2 AA
With scope, methods and participants, and its limits stated
As time-on-task and satisfaction scores only
rationale: W3C warns against generalizing from a small number of participants. Small studies are valuable but not statistically robust. Reports should explain the scope, methods and who took part, and say clearly that results don't represent all people with disabilities. For accessibility-focused sessions, W3C suggests a think-aloud approach and focusing on errors caused by barriers, rather than time-on-task or satisfaction scores.

distractors.0: Three participants can't support statistical claims about everyone.
distractors.1: User testing doesn't establish WCAG conformance; that needs a conformance evaluation.
distractors.3: W3C suggests focusing on barrier-related errors rather than time-on-task or satisfaction in accessibility sessions.

sources.title: W3C WAI: Involving Users in Evaluating Web Accessibility
sources.note: Tips for running studies and reporting results.

question: W3C publishes supplemental guidance for people with cognitive and learning disabilities, such as helping users focus and designing processes that don't rely on memory. How does it relate to WCAG conformance?
options: It replaces WCAG for content aimed at cognitive disabilities
It goes beyond WCAG and isn't required for conformance
It becomes required once a site claims Level AA
It applies only to government and public sector sites
rationale: Many needs of people with cognitive and learning disabilities are hard to express as testable success criteria, so WCAG covers only some of them. W3C's supplemental guidance, based on the Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force's "Making Content Usable" work, gives objectives and design patterns such as clear content, helping users find what they need, avoiding mistakes and supporting personalization. It isn't required for WCAG conformance, but following it makes content more usable for many people.

distractors.0: It supplements WCAG; it doesn't replace it.
distractors.2: W3C describes it as additional guidance not required for conformance at any level.
distractors.3: It applies to any content, not only government sites.

tip: Meeting WCAG doesn't guarantee content works well for everyone, especially people with cognitive disabilities. Supplemental guidance and user testing fill the gap.

sources.title: W3C WAI: Supplemental Guidance to WCAG 2
sources.note: Cognitive accessibility objectives and design patterns beyond WCAG.
